questions.q:
Find the mistake in each statement written by a Class 6 student and correct it.
(i) 'The IAU listed the 88 constellations in ancient times.'
(ii) 'Canis Major is pictured as the hunter, and Orion as his dog.'
(iii) 'Once the magnetic compass was invented, recognising star patterns stopped being of any use for finding direction.'
questions.a: (i) The IAU defined the agreed constellation boundaries in the early twentieth century, not in ancient times. (ii) It is the other way round: Orion is pictured as the hunter and Canis Major as his dog. (iii) Recognising stars and their patterns is still used in emergencies as a backup method for finding direction.
s: (i) the IAU list is from the early twentieth century
(ii) Orion is the hunter, Canis Major the dog
(iii) still used as a backup method in emergencies

questions.q: Meera in Kerala and Tenzin in Ladakh look at the same group of bright stars. Meera joins them into a fishing boat; Tenzin joins them into a plough. Which conclusion fits what the chapter says about star patterns?
questions.a: Both are valid, as each culture shaped patterns from its own stories
o: Both are valid, as each culture shaped patterns from its own stories
Only one can be right, since a group of stars has one true shape
They must be seeing different stars, as Kerala and Ladakh share no sky
Both are wrong, because only the official IAU pictures may be drawn

questions.q:
Each clue in Column I points to a star, and the star belongs to a constellation in Column II. Match each clue to the constellation.
Column I | Column II
1. Holds the star that stays nearly fixed in the north | a. Canis Major
2. Holds the brightest star of the night sky | b. Ursa Major
3. Its three middle stars form a short straight row | c. Ursa Minor
4. Holds the dipper whose cup stars point to the Pole Star | d. Orion

At a star-story evening in Bengaluru, a guide points to three neighbouring constellations: a hunter, a dog behind him and a bull he is battling.
(a) Name the constellation that is the dog and the one that is the bull.
(b) Asha says, 'Sirius is one of the three stars of the hunter's belt, since it lies so close to Orion.' Correct her, using (a).
questions.a: (a) The dog is Canis Major and the bull is Taurus (the hunter is Orion). (b) Sirius is not a belt star. It belongs to Canis Major, the dog constellation named in (a); it only lies close to Orion. Orion's belt is three stars in a short straight line in the middle of Orion.
s: Part (a): dog = Canis Major, bull = Taurus
Part (b): Sirius belongs to Canis Major, not to Orion's belt; it is only near Orion

questions.q: Plan a 20-minute 'stories in the stars' session for Class 3 children at your school. Give five steps, one for each of these ideas: (1) the lines joining stars are imaginary; (2) different people and cultures make different patterns from the same stars; (3) Orion, Canis Major and Taurus; (4) the IAU's 88 regions; (5) stars used to find direction. For each step, say what the children will do and the correct idea it teaches.
questions.a: Five steps, one per idea, e.g. (1) Show a picture of bright stars and let children join them with lines; explain the lines are imaginary, drawn only to help identify the stars. (2) Compare their shapes and stories: different people, like different cultures, make different patterns from the same stars. (3) Show Orion as a hunter with a three-star belt, Canis Major as his dog with Sirius, the brightest star of the night sky, and Taurus as the bull. (4) Explain that long ago constellations meant star patterns, but the IAU in the early twentieth century divided the whole sky into 88 regions, which are now the constellations. (5) Tell how sailors and travellers used stars like the Pole Star, which stays nearly fixed in the north, to find direction before the compass.
s: Step on imaginary lines joining stars, with an activity
Step on different people/cultures making different patterns and stories
Step naming Orion (hunter), Canis Major (dog, with Sirius) and Taurus (bull) correctly
Step on the IAU dividing the whole sky into 88 regions in the early twentieth century
Step on stars used for direction (e.g. the Pole Star nearly fixed in the north)

questions.q: Riya's star chart shows Orion joined by red lines. On a very dark night in Spiti she finds Orion's stars but cannot see any of the lines between them. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: The lines are imagined, drawn on charts only to help us
o: The lines are imagined, drawn on charts only to help us
The lines are seen only through a telescope or binoculars
The lines are visible only from the southern hemisphere
Moonlight was hiding the lines that join Orion's stars

questions.q: A student finds an old star map from one culture that showed 36 star patterns across the whole sky. The International Astronomical Union's official list now divides the entire sky into regions called constellations. The IAU list has ___ more regions than that old map had patterns. (Write a number.)
True or False? 'Every star shines with its own light, so all the stars we see at night look equally bright.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Stars do shine with their own light, but some look bright and others dim. For example, Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, while the Pole Star is not very bright.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: some stars look bright and some dim, e.g. Sirius very bright, Pole Star not very bright

questions.q:
A museum in Jaipur shows three charts of the same patch of the northern sky, each marking one bright star, X.
Chart | Made by | What it shows around star X
A | an old farming community | X is one of 7 stars joined into a plough; the plough's outline is drawn as the boundary
B | an old travelling community | X is one of 4 stars joined into a bow; the bow's outline is drawn as the boundary
C | a 2026 atlas that follows the IAU | X lies inside a marked region named Ursa Major, along with many fainter stars that belong to no picture
(a) Why do Charts A and B join the same stars into different pictures?
(b) Which chart uses today's meaning of 'constellation' and which use the older meaning?
(c) Chart A's makers had no magnetic compass. Apart from telling stories, what real use could their plough pattern have had?
(d) The museum can print one caption for visitors from many countries saying which constellation X belongs to. One guide wants Chart A, since its plough story helped local people recognise these stars for centuries; another wants Chart C. Decide, weighing both sides.
questions.a: (a) The lines joining stars are imaginary, and each culture shaped the stars into familiar things from its own stories, so the same stars became a plough for one and a bow for the other. (b) Chart C uses today's meaning: a constellation is a defined region of the sky. Charts A and B use the older meaning: a group of stars forming a pattern. (c) Recognising the pattern helped them recognise particular stars, and recognising stars helped people find directions on land before the magnetic compass. (d) Chart C. Different cultures drew constellation boundaries in different ways (A and B do not even agree on which stars go with X), which is exactly why the IAU defined one agreed set of boundaries for the whole sky; only C gives every visitor the same answer. The plough story is still worth telling as the local pattern, but not as the boundary of the constellation.
s: Part (a): lines are imaginary; each culture made shapes from its own stories
Part (b): C = region of sky (today); A and B = pattern of stars (older)
Part (c): recognising stars to find direction before the compass
Part (d): Chart C, because cultures' boundaries differed and the IAU set one agreed set; the story can stay as the local pattern

questions.q: Three travellers each need to find direction without a phone: (1) a caravan crossing Nubra in ancient days, (2) a sailor at sea before the magnetic compass was invented, (3) a trekking group in Uttarakhand today whose GPS and compass have both failed. According to the chapter, which of them could use known stars and their patterns to find direction?
questions.a: All three of them
o: All three of them
Only 1 and 2, since star finding ended once the compass came
Only 2, since stars helped people find direction only at sea
Only 3, since people long ago had no names for star patterns

questions.q:
A 2026 star atlas says that a faint star, which is not part of the hunter pattern at all, 'lies in Orion'.
(a) How can a star outside the hunter pattern still be in Orion today?
(b) Why do people still say 'Orion' for the hunter pattern itself?
questions.a: (a) Today a constellation is a defined region of the sky. Orion is the region that includes the hunter pattern, so any star inside that region, even one not in the pattern, lies in Orion. (b) In constellations the pattern of stars is usually the most noticeable feature, so the word constellation is still commonly used for the group of stars forming the pattern.
s: Part (a): a constellation is now a region of sky, so any star inside the region is in Orion
Part (b): the pattern is the most noticeable part, so the name is still used for the pattern

questions.q:
A Class 6 quiz card makes three statements about star patterns.
Statement 1: The three stars in the middle of Orion are imagined as the hunter's belt.
Statement 2: The Pole Star is part of the Big Dipper, which lies in Ursa Major.
Statement 3: The Big Dipper lies in the constellation Ursa Major.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is: 'Look in Ursa Minor, not in Ursa Major.' Write a question about the night sky for which this is the correct answer, and explain why Ursa Major is the tempting wrong answer.
questions.a: Example question: 'In which constellation will you find the Pole Star?' (or 'Which constellation holds the Little Dipper?'). The Pole Star is part of the Little Dipper, which lies in Ursa Minor. Ursa Major is tempting because it holds the Big Dipper, whose cup stars are used to find the Pole Star, but the Pole Star itself is not in it.
s: A question whose answer is Ursa Minor (Pole Star or Little Dipper)
Pole Star is part of the Little Dipper, in Ursa Minor
Ursa Major tempts because the Big Dipper there is used to point to the Pole Star

questions.q:
Assertion (A): On a clear winter night, Sirius stands out far more brightly than the Pole Star.
Reason (R): Sirius belongs to the constellation Canis Major, which some people imagine as the dog that follows the hunter Orion.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: 'In the olden days, star patterns were a traveller's map and compass.' Justify this statement in five points, using the chapter. Include one limit on using stars to find direction.
questions.a: (1) Star patterns looked like familiar shapes, so they helped people recognise particular stars in the sky. (2) Before modern technology, and even before the magnetic compass, recognising stars helped sailors and travellers find directions at sea and on land. (3) The Pole Star appears nearly stationary in the north, so finding it gave the north direction in the northern hemisphere. (4) Caravans passing through Nubra in Ladakh were helped by particular stars to find their way, and the skill is still used as a backup in emergencies. (5) Limit: it needs a clear night, and the Pole Star cannot be seen from the southern hemisphere.
s: Patterns helped recognise particular stars
Used by sailors and travellers before the compass to find direction
Pole Star nearly fixed in the north gives north in the northern hemisphere
Caravan example or still a backup in emergencies
A limit: clear sky needed, or Pole Star not visible from the southern hemisphere

questions.q:
Yangdol says the stars over Nubra glow only because sunlight falls on them, the way sunlight lights up the Moon.
(a) Is she right about the stars? Give the reason from the chapter.
(b) Name one object in the night sky that does shine only by reflecting sunlight, and say how it differs from a star.
questions.a: (a) No. Stars shine with their own light. (b) The Moon (or a planet such as Venus). It does not make its own light; it shines because of the sunlight it reflects, while a star gives out its own light.
s: Part (a): no, stars shine with their own light
Part (b): the Moon or a planet, which only reflects sunlight

questions.q: Sonu sketches the northern sky at 9 p.m. and again at 1 a.m. His two sketches show the Big Dipper in different places, but one nearby star, not very bright, is in the same place in both. Which star is this most likely to be?
questions.a: The Pole Star of the Little Dipper
o: The Pole Star of the Little Dipper
Sirius, the dog star of Canis Major
The last star in the Big Dipper's cup
The middle star of Orion's belt

questions.q: Nisha claims: 'There are exactly 88 constellations because people of all ancient cultures agreed on the same 88 star patterns.' Check her claim. Is it right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The number 88 is correct: 88 constellations are officially listed. But they did not come from an ancient agreement. Different cultures had their own patterns and drew constellation boundaries in different ways, so in the early twentieth century the International Astronomical Union (IAU) defined an agreed set of boundaries, dividing the entire sky into 88 regions. These regions are what are now called constellations.
s: Verdict: partly right (88 is correct, the reason is wrong)
Cultures had different patterns and boundaries, not one agreed set
The IAU divided the whole sky into 88 regions in the early twentieth century

questions.q:
On a cloudless December night in Leh, a Class 6 group sketches three star patterns and notes what they see:
Pattern | What the group noted
P | Three bright stars in a short straight row, with other bright stars above and below them; the group says it looks like a man with a belt
Q | Lies close to P; holds a star that is brighter than every other star they saw that night
R | A small dipper-shaped group in the northern sky; one star in it, not very bright, seems to stay in the same place all night
(a) Name the constellation P and the bright star in Q.
(b) Name the dipper-shaped group R and its star that stays in place.
(c) Dolkar wants one star from the log to find north on tomorrow's trek. Which star should she use and why not the brightest one? Decide.
questions.a: (a) P is Orion (the three stars are the hunter's belt); the bright star in Q is Sirius, in Canis Major. (b) R is the Little Dipper (in Ursa Minor) and the star is the Pole Star (Polaris). (c) She should use the Pole Star. It appears nearly stationary in the north direction, so it marks north in the northern hemisphere. Sirius is the brightest, but brightness does not show direction: it does not stay in the north.
s: Part (a): P is Orion and the star is Sirius
Part (b): Little Dipper and the Pole Star
Part (c): the Pole Star, because it stays nearly fixed in the north; Sirius is bright but does not mark north

questions.q:
A shepherd in old Nubra could not read a chart, but he knew the night sky by its shapes.
(a) Why would joining certain stars into a familiar shape help him pick out the same stars night after night?
(b) On a hazy night only a few stars showed. Why would a shape made of bright stars serve him better than one made of dim stars?
questions.a: (a) Imaginary shapes like familiar things helped people recognise stars in the sky: once he saw the shape, he knew which stars he was looking at, every night. (b) Some stars are bright and others dim; in haze the dim stars are the first to disappear, so a shape built from bright stars can still be recognised when the dim ones cannot be seen.
s: Part (a): the familiar shape helps recognise the same stars
Part (b): stars differ in brightness; dim ones vanish first in haze, bright ones still show

questions.q: A poster at a school science fair says: 'The Big Dipper is one of the 88 constellations.' Using today's meaning of the word, which correction is best?
questions.a: The Big Dipper is a pattern lying inside Ursa Major
o: The Big Dipper is a pattern lying inside Ursa Major
The Big Dipper is the constellation that holds the Pole Star
The Big Dipper is a group of planets lying in Ursa Minor
The Big Dipper is part of Orion, just above the hunter's belt

questions.q: In February, Rohan finds the three belt stars of Orion and imagines a straight line through them. He follows the line towards the west and finds no very bright star. What should he have done?
questions.a: Followed the same line towards the east
o: Followed the same line towards the east
Used the two end stars of the Big Dipper
Looked inside the belt, between its stars
Waited for the Moon to rise and help him

questions.q:
Rhea lives in Indore. From her terrace she has an open view of the eastern, southern and western sky, but a tall water tank blocks the whole northern sky.
(a) On a June night at 9 p.m., which search will the tank spoil: finding the Big Dipper and the Pole Star, or finding a bright star overhead? Give the reason.
(b) What kind of place should she move to instead?
questions.a: (a) Finding the Big Dipper and the Pole Star. The Big Dipper is looked for in the northern part of the sky in summer around 9 p.m., and the Pole Star appears in the north, so the tank blocks both. (b) An open, dark area away from lights, tall buildings and trees, with a clear view of the northern sky.
s: Part (a): the Big Dipper/Pole Star search, because both are in the northern sky
Part (b): an open dark place away from lights, buildings and trees

questions.q: On a printed photo of the summer night sky, the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup are 3 cm apart. Following the chapter's method, the Pole Star should lie about ___ cm away from them along the straight line through them.
Your class in Hyderabad wants to hold a night sky watching session to find the Big Dipper and the Pole Star. Plan it in five steps. For each step, give the reason the chapter offers.
questions.a: (1) Go with adults to a dark open area away from lights, tall buildings and trees, because light pollution and obstructions reduce what can be seen. (2) Use a sky-mapping app to choose the date and time, because not all stars are visible from every place on every night; for the Big Dipper, a summer night around 9 p.m., looking at the northern sky. (3) Pick a night with no Moon and no clouds, because the Pole Star is not very bright. (4) Carry a magnetic compass to find directions, printouts or an app map of the patterns, and a notebook to note or draw observations. (5) On arrival, wait about half an hour so that the eyes adjust to the dark and the sky is seen better.
s: Dark open place with adults, away from lights, buildings and trees
App to choose date and time (summer, about 9 p.m., northern sky)
Moonless, cloudless night because the Pole Star is dim
Compass, star maps and notebook, each with its use
Wait about half an hour for the eyes to adjust

questions.q: A school group reaches a dark field outside Nashik at 7:50 p.m. The bus home leaves at 9:15 p.m. The teacher follows the chapter's advice on getting the eyes ready, and then wants 40 minutes of star-spotting. Will the plan fit before the bus leaves?
questions.a: Yes, with 15 minutes to spare
o: Yes, with 15 minutes to spare
Yes, with 45 minutes to spare
No, it will be 15 minutes short
Yes, with 85 minutes to spare

questions.q: True or False? 'On the same cloudless night, a child on a brightly lit city street will see fewer stars than her cousin in a dark village field nearby, even though the same sky is above both of them.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The stars are the same, but the city street has light pollution, excessive artificial light at night, which makes many stars hard to see. Where there is less light pollution, as in villages, a larger number of stars can be seen.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: light pollution in the city hides many stars; less light pollution in the village shows more

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For a Pole Star search, the teacher picks a night when neither the Moon nor clouds are in the sky.
Reason (R): The Pole Star is not a very bright star.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: On a clear January evening just after sunset, a beginner in Nagpur can try only one search: Orion, or the Pole Star found through the Big Dipper. Which search does the chapter's timing advice support for that evening? Give one reason about each search.
questions.a: Orion. (1) In India, Orion is best viewed from December to April after sunset, so a January evening just after sunset is inside its best period. (2) The chapter's search for the Big Dipper, which leads to the Pole Star, is set for summer time in the early part of the night, around 9 p.m., not for a winter evening just after sunset.
s: Orion: January after sunset is inside the December to April viewing period
Pole Star: the chapter's Big Dipper search is set for summer around 9 p.m.

questions.q:
Students in Ooty have a printed photo of the northern sky taken on a summer night. They draw a straight line through the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup, which are 2.5 cm apart on the photo, and carry it on towards the north. Three stars that are not very bright lie on or near this line:
Star | Distance along the line from the cup stars
X | 6 cm
Y | 12.5 cm
Z | 20 cm
(a) Decide first: which star is the Pole Star? Show the check.
(b) On a larger print of the same sky, the Pole Star is 18 cm from the cup stars. Work backwards: how far apart are the two cup stars on that print?
(c) On a small pocket card, the cup stars are 1.8 cm apart and the card has only 8 cm of space beyond them along this line. Can the Pole Star appear on the card? Show the check, and name the direction the line points.
questions.a: (a) Y. The Pole Star is about five times the distance between the cup stars: 5 x 2.5 = 12.5 cm, which is Y. (b) 18 / 5 = 3.6 cm apart. (c) No. 5 x 1.8 = 9 cm, which is more than the 8 cm of space, so the Pole Star falls off the card. The line points towards the north.
s: Part (a): Y, since 5 x 2.5 = 12.5 cm
Part (c): 5 x 1.8 = 9 cm > 8 cm, so no; the line points north

questions.q:
A club in Jaipur is planning a night to find the Pole Star. Members make three suggestions.
Statement 1: Pick a night with a bright full Moon, since moonlight will help us spot dim stars.
Statement 2: Before going, we should use a sky-mapping app to choose the date and time for this search.
Statement 3: A garden ringed by tall trees is fine, as long as no lamps are on.
Which suggestions agree with the chapter?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q: Lerato lives in Cape Town, which is in the southern hemisphere. She writes to her pen pal in Bhopal: 'From my backyard I used the Big Dipper's cup stars, went about five times their distance, and found the Pole Star.' Show that her report cannot be right.
questions.a: Cape Town is in the southern hemisphere. The chapter says the Pole Star is not visible from the southern hemisphere of Earth. So, whatever star she reached, it cannot be the Pole Star; the method of finding the Pole Star from the Big Dipper works only where the Pole Star can be seen, in the northern hemisphere.
s: Cape Town is in the southern hemisphere (from the stem)
The Pole Star is not visible from the southern hemisphere
So the star she found cannot be the Pole Star; the method works only in the northern hemisphere

questions.q: Priya in Chennai wants to see the constellation Orion together with as many of the fainter stars around it as possible. Which plan gives her the best chance?
questions.a: A clear, moonless February night, from an open field outside the city
o: A clear, moonless February night, from an open field outside the city
A clear, full-Moon February night, from an open field outside the city
A clear, moonless August night, from an open field outside the city
A clear, moonless February night, from her terrace in the city centre

questions.q:
Match what a sky-watcher wants to do (Column I) with the first step the chapter suggests (Column II).
Column I | Column II
1. Find north once the Pole Star has been spotted | a. Look for three bright stars in a short straight row
2. Find Orion quickly | b. Follow the line through Orion's belt towards the east
3. Find the dim Pole Star | c. Face the Pole Star, which stays nearly fixed in the north
4. Find the brightest star of the night sky | d. Extend the line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper's cup

Ritu, in Shimla, goes out on a June night at about 9 p.m. to find the Big Dipper and then the Pole Star.
(a) Towards which part of the sky should she face to find the Big Dipper?
(b) Using (a), explain why she does not need to turn around to look for the Pole Star once the Big Dipper is found.
questions.a: (a) The northern part of the sky, above the horizon. (b) The line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper's cup is followed towards the north, and the Pole Star appears nearly stationary in the north direction, so it is in the same part of the sky she is already facing.
s: Part (a): the northern sky
Part (b): the cup line runs north and the Pole Star is in the north, the same side she faces

questions.q: Sana says: 'The only reason people in big cities see so few stars is light pollution.' Is her claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right (a verdict of 'wrong, because of the word only' is also accepted when the other causes are given). Light pollution (excessive artificial light at night) is a real reason. But the chapter also gives smoke and dust in city air as reasons the sky is rarely clear, and tall buildings and trees around a house can block the view. So light pollution is not the only reason.
s: Verdict: partly right, or wrong because of 'only'; light pollution is a reason but not the only one
Light pollution = excessive artificial light at night
Other reasons: smoke and dust, and tall buildings and trees blocking the view

questions.q: Yangdol, in Nubra (Ladakh), sees thousands of stars at night. Her cousin Kabir, in a big city, sees only a few from his flat. Compare their skies on five points from the chapter and conclude what Kabir could change and what he could not change on his own.
questions.a: (1) Clouds: Nubra's weather is almost cloudless; a city sky is rarely clear. (2) Air: Nubra has almost no air pollution; city air has smoke and dust. (3) Light: Nubra has almost no light pollution; the city has excessive artificial light at night. (4) View: Kabir's flat may be surrounded by tall buildings and trees that block his view of the sky. (5) Conclusion: Kabir can move to an open, dark area away from lights and buildings (with adults) and wait for his eyes to adjust, but he cannot by himself remove the city's light pollution, smoke and dust.
s: Clouds: almost cloudless vs rarely clear
Air: almost no air pollution vs smoke and dust
Light pollution: almost none vs excessive artificial light
View blocked by tall buildings and trees in the city
Conclusion: he can move to a dark open place, but cannot remove the city's light pollution alone

questions.q: On four cloudless nights, a student in Mysuru sees fewer stars than usual. Each option gives the cause on one of those nights. Which night's cause is light pollution?
questions.a: Stadium floodlights are on next door
o: Stadium floodlights are on next door
A bright full Moon is high in the sky
A tall neem tree hides most of the sky
She watched without waiting in the dark

questions.q:
An eco-club in Pune looks at the sky through the same small cardboard frame and counts the stars inside it, from four spots. Each time the sky is cloudless.
Spot | Count
P: school terrace, street lights on | 8
Q: same terrace, during a power cut | 19
R: village field 25 km away, no Moon | 64
S: same field, full Moon up | 21
The school terrace has a tall water tank on its northern side.
(a) Which two spots, compared, show the effect of light pollution most fairly? What is light pollution?
(b) How many times as many stars were counted at R as at P?
(c) On the night at S, the club wanted to find both Orion's belt and the Pole Star. Which one was more likely to be missed, and why?
(d) The club will hold one Pole Star night. Should it be at the terrace during a power cut or at the field on a moonless night? Decide, using the data and the terrace's layout.
questions.a: (a) P and Q: same place, same sky, only the street lights differ. Light pollution is the presence of excessive artificial light at night. (b) 64 / 8 = 8 times as many. (c) The Pole Star. It is not very bright, so with the Moon lighting the sky it is hard to see; Orion's belt is made of three bright stars. (d) The field on a moonless night. It gave the highest count (64), and the terrace's tank blocks the northern sky, which is exactly where the Pole Star is found.
s: Part (a): P and Q, and light pollution = excessive artificial light at night
Part (b): 8 times
Part (c): the Pole Star, as it is not very bright
Part (d): the field on a moonless night: highest count, and the tank blocks the north

questions.q: A sky-watching guide gives this advice: 'Move away from the tall buildings; the lights are not your problem here.' Describe a situation in which this is the right advice, and explain why it is right and why moving away from lights alone would not help.
questions.a: Example: a group stands in an unlit courtyard during a power cut, in a new housing colony, with tall apartment blocks on all sides; they see only a small patch of sky overhead. It is right because the courtyard is already dark, so light pollution is not the problem; the tall buildings block the view of most of the sky. Moving to a darker spot that is still enclosed by buildings would not show more of the sky; an open dark area would.
s: A situation that is dark but enclosed by tall buildings
Light pollution is not the cause there, since the place is dark
The buildings block the view; an open dark area is needed

questions.q: Ayaan, in Kolkata, cannot find a constellation he read about. He says: 'If a constellation is not in my sky tonight, it must be clouds or city lights hiding it.' Is he right? Give two reasons, other than clouds or city lights, why he may not see it.
questions.a: No, not necessarily. (1) Not all stars and constellations are visible on all nights of the year; for example, Orion is best viewed in India from December to April, so in another season it may not be in the evening sky. (2) Tall buildings or trees around him may block the part of the sky where it is (and some constellations are not visible from every place on Earth at all).
s: Verdict: no, there can be other reasons
Not every constellation is visible on every night of the year

s: Part (a): Tray 2, as the Moon has no atmosphere, water or life

Part (d): not supported; the tray hit more often kept fewer pits, so wearing away decides how many last

questions.q:
A student writes three statements for a poster on natural satellites.
Statement 1: Mars has one moon, just like the Earth.
Statement 2: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune each have a large number of moons.
Statement 3: Moons are natural satellites, and satellites are smaller than the planets they move around.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Meena claims: 'In one year of 365 days, the Moon completes at least 13 full trips around the Earth, but not 14.' Check her claim with working.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. The Moon takes about 27 days for one revolution around the Earth. 13 x 27 = 351 days, which is less than 365, so 13 full trips fit. 14 x 27 = 378 days, which is more than 365, so the 14th trip is not finished (365 / 27 = about 13.5).
s: The Moon takes about 27 days per revolution
Verdict: yes, 13 full trips but not 14

questions.q:
A Class 6 student writes a story about a Moon base. Judge each sentence as correct or incorrect, using the chapter, and correct the wrong ones.
(i) 'From our base we watched the Earth's other moon rise.'
(ii) 'A gentle wind on the Moon slowly filled the old craters with dust.'
(iii) 'The Moon took about 27 days to go once around the Earth.'
(iv) 'Through our telescope we watched Jupiter, which has just one moon, like the Earth.'
(v) 'Our base was near the Moon's south pole, the little-explored region where India's Vikram lander set down in 2023.'
questions.a: (i) Incorrect: the Earth has only one Moon. (ii) Incorrect: the Moon has hardly any atmosphere, and the chapter says that with no atmosphere, water or life, craters stay on the Moon's surface for a very long time. (iii) Correct: about 27 days. (iv) Incorrect: Jupiter has a large number of moons; it is the Earth that has one. (v) Correct: Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander soft-landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.
s: (i) incorrect, the Earth has one Moon
(ii) incorrect, hardly any atmosphere, craters last a very long time
(iii) correct, about 27 days
(iv) incorrect, Jupiter has a large number of moons
(v) correct, Vikram landed near the south pole in 2023

questions.q:
Deepa says, 'The Moon is our nearest neighbour in space, so it must be the brightest object in our sky.'
(a) Is she right? Use what the chapter says about the brightest objects.
(b) Does the Moon make its own light? Explain.
questions.a: (a) No. The Sun is the brightest object; the chapter says Venus is the brightest object after the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon comes after the Sun. Being nearest does not make it the brightest. (b) No. The Sun produces almost all the energy in the Solar System; the Moon, like the other objects in it, shines due to the sunlight it reflects from its surface.
s: Part (a): no, the Sun is brighter; the Moon comes after the Sun
Part (b): no, it shines by reflecting sunlight

questions.q: A comet with a long tail was easy to see from Pune in January. By May the same comet could no longer be seen without a telescope. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: It had moved away from the Sun, so it appeared dim
o: It had moved away from the Sun, so it appeared dim
It had stopped revolving and stayed still in space
It had lost all of its ice and turned into a planet
It had become a star that shines only in the daytime

questions.q:
An observatory tracks two objects for a year.
Object M: rocky and irregular in shape, about 2 km across; it shows no tail even at its closest to the Sun.
Object N: only a faint dot when far from the Sun; as it nears the Sun it brightens and grows a long tail.
(a) Name each object and give the feature from the chapter that decides it.
(b) Rohan says, 'At 2 km wide, M is far too big to be an asteroid.' Check his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) M is an asteroid: a small rocky object of irregular shape, with no tail. N is a comet: comets have long tails that form near the Sun and appear dim when away from it. (b) Rohan is wrong. Asteroids range from 10 m to about 500 km across, and 2 km lies well inside that range (2 km = 2,000 m, more than 10 m and far less than 500 km).
s: Part (a): M an asteroid (rocky, irregular, no tail); N a comet (tail near the Sun, dim far away)
Part (b): wrong; asteroids are 10 m to about 500 km, and 2 km is within the range

questions.q: Halley's Comet appears about every 76 years, and it was last seen in 1986. So the appearance before 1986 was in about the year ___.
A website describes 'a nearly spherical, rocky asteroid 700 km wide that moves around Jupiter'. Show that this object cannot be an asteroid, giving three separate reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: (1) Size: asteroids are from 10 m to about 500 km across; 700 km is larger than that. (2) Shape: asteroids are irregular in shape; this object is nearly spherical. (3) Motion: a body that moves around Jupiter moves around a planet, so it is a satellite (a moon of Jupiter), not an asteroid; the asteroids the chapter describes revolve around the Sun.
s: Too big: asteroids are 10 m to about 500 km
Wrong shape: asteroids are irregular, not nearly spherical
Wrong motion: an object moving around a planet (Jupiter) is a satellite, a moon

questions.q:
Read three statements about the small objects of the Solar System.
Statement 1: Comets are made up of dust, gases, rocks and ice.
Statement 2: Comets come from the inner region of the Solar System, near Mercury and Venus.
Statement 3: Asteroids are nearly spherical in shape, like the planets.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 2 only

questions.q:
A school in Nagpur is building hanging models of the largest and the smallest asteroids that the chapter describes, for a hall 10 m long. Two scales are suggested: Scale A, 1 cm stands for 10 km; Scale B, 1 cm stands for 100 m.
(a) How wide is the model of the largest asteroid at Scale A?
(b) How wide is the same model at Scale B? (1 km = 1,000 m)
(c) Which scale lets the largest asteroid model fit in the hall? Decide.
(d) At the scale you chose, how wide would the model of the smallest asteroid be? What does this tell you about making it?
(e) Planet models already hang in the hall. What shape should the asteroid models have, and how will that make them look different from the planet models? Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: The chapter gives asteroid sizes from 10 m to about 500 km. (a) 500 / 10 = 50 cm. (b) 500 km = 5,00,000 m; 5,00,000 / 100 = 5,000 cm = 50 m. (c) Scale A: 50 cm fits easily in a 10 m hall, while at Scale B the model would be 50 m, five times the hall's length. (d) 10 m = 0.01 km, and 0.01 / 10 = 0.001 cm, far too small to make or see; the smallest asteroids are tiny compared with the largest, so they cannot be shown at the same scale. (e) Irregular, lumpy shapes, because asteroids are rocky and irregular in shape, while the planet models should be nearly spherical, as the Sun and the planets are.
s: Part (a): 50 cm (largest asteroid about 500 km)
Part (b): 5,000 cm = 50 m
Part (c): Scale A, since 50 cm fits and 50 m does not
Part (d): smallest about 10 m, so 0.001 cm, too small to make; sizes range very widely
Part (e): irregular shapes, unlike the nearly spherical planets

questions.q: True or False? 'All asteroids stay inside the belt between Mars and Jupiter, so no asteroid ever comes near the Earth.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Many asteroids revolve around the Sun in paths between those of Mars and Jupiter (the asteroid belt), but not all stay far away: occasionally some asteroids pass very close to the Earth.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: many are in the belt, but occasionally some pass very close to the Earth

questions.q: A survey finds four rocky, irregular objects revolving around the Sun. Using the chapter's size range for asteroids, which one could NOT be an asteroid?
questions.a: A rock about 2 m across
o: A rock about 2 m across
A body about 15 km across
A body about 450 km across
A rock about 60 m across

questions.q:
(a) Arrange these in order of distance from the Sun, nearest first: Jupiter, the asteroid belt, Earth, Mars.
(b) Ravi says the asteroid belt lies beyond Jupiter, among the giant planets. Correct him, and say what the asteroids in the belt are like.
questions.a: (a) Earth, Mars, the asteroid belt, Jupiter. (b) The belt is not beyond Jupiter: many asteroids revolve around the Sun in paths that lie between those of Mars and Jupiter. They are small, rocky objects of irregular shape.
s: Part (a): Earth, Mars, asteroid belt, Jupiter
Part (b): between Mars and Jupiter; small, rocky and irregular

questions.q:
An observatory in Ladakh follows a newly found object on its way through the Solar System. Its notes:
Month | Where it is | What is seen
January | far out, moving towards the Sun | a faint dot, no tail
March | closest to the Sun | bright, with a long tail
May | moving away from the Sun | tail getting shorter
August | far from the Sun again | cannot be seen with the naked eye; the observatory's big telescope still picks it up as a faint dot
A sample study says the object is made of dust, gases, rocks and ice.
(a) Is this object an asteroid or a comet? Give one clue from the notes and one from the sample study.
(b) From the notes, how is the object's distance from the Sun linked to how bright it looks?
(c) In March some villagers were afraid that the bright object with a tail would bring bad luck. What do scientists now say such objects are?
(d) A school club wants a photo of the long tail. It can either use the observatory's big telescope for one night in late August, or set up its own simple camera for one night in early March. Which should it choose? Weigh the telescope's power against what the notes show.
questions.a: (a) A comet: the notes show a long tail near the Sun, and the sample shows dust, gases, rocks and ice, what comets are made of. (b) It looks brightest when it is closest to the Sun (March) and grows dim as it moves away; far from the Sun it cannot be seen with the naked eye. (c) In many cultures comets have been feared, but scientists now know they are just icy-rocky visitors making a trip close to the Sun. (d) Early March with the simple camera. The big telescope can show dim objects, but the tail is formed only when the comet is close to the Sun and its frozen material evaporates; in late August, far from the Sun, there is no long tail left to photograph, only a faint dot.
s: Part (a): a comet, from the tail and the make-up
Part (b): brightest nearest the Sun, dim as it moves away
Part (c): icy-rocky visitors making a trip close to the Sun, not bringers of bad luck
Part (d): early March, as the tail exists only near the Sun; the telescope cannot show a tail that is not there

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A comet that was a faint dot with no tail far from the Sun shows a long tail when it comes close to the Sun.
Reason (R): As a comet approaches close to the Sun, the frozen material in it starts evaporating.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) Asteroids revolve around the Sun, yet they are not called planets. Give two differences from the chapter.
(b) Is the Earth's Moon an asteroid, given that it is rocky and covered in craters? Explain.
questions.a: (a) A planet is large and nearly spherical; asteroids are small and irregular in shape. (b) No. The Moon revolves around the Earth, so it is the Earth's natural satellite; asteroids revolve around the Sun, not around a planet.
s: Part (a): planets are large and nearly spherical; asteroids small and irregular
Part (b): no, the Moon revolves around the Earth, so it is a satellite

questions.q: Arun says: 'A comet is just a star with a tail. It glows in the sky, so it must make its own light like a star.' Is his claim right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: No. A comet is not a star: it is a visitor from the outer regions of the Solar System, made up of dust, gases, rocks and ice. It does not make its own light; except for the Sun, all objects in the Solar System shine due to the sunlight they reflect from their surfaces. Stars, like the Sun, shine with their own light.
s: Verdict: no, a comet is not a star
A comet is an icy-rocky visitor from the outer Solar System (dust, gases, rocks and ice)
It shines by reflecting sunlight; stars shine with their own light

questions.q: A news report says astronomers have tracked a rocky, potato-shaped body about 300 km long. It revolves around the Sun and shows no tail even at its closest to the Sun. What is it most likely to be?
questions.a: An asteroid
o: An asteroid
A comet from the outer regions
A dwarf planet just like Pluto
A natural satellite of Mars

questions.q:
A museum gives five clue cards. Each card has one feature that could trick you. Name the kind of object each card describes (planet, dwarf planet, natural satellite, asteroid or comet), and say which clue decides it and why the tricky feature does not.
(i) Rocky and covered in craters; about a quarter of the Earth's diameter; moves around the Earth.
(ii) Revolves around the Sun beyond Neptune; once called a planet; smaller than the Earth's Moon.
(iii) Shone brightly near the Sun this March; far from the Sun it is only a faint dot; made of dust, gases, rocks and ice.
(iv) Rocky; about 200 km across; irregular in shape; revolves around the Sun.
(v) Revolves around the Sun; mostly gas and ice; has flat ring-like structures; shines only by reflected sunlight.
questions.a: (i) Natural satellite (the Moon): it moves around the Earth, a planet. Being rocky and cratered does not make it an asteroid, as asteroids revolve around the Sun. (ii) Dwarf planet (Pluto): since the IAU's 2006 definition, smaller objects like Pluto are called dwarf planets. Revolving around the Sun and once being called a planet do not make it one today. (iii) Comet: made of dust, gases, rocks and ice and bright near the Sun. Shining brightly does not make it a star; comets appear dim as they move away from the Sun. (iv) Asteroid: small, rocky, irregular, revolving around the Sun. Being 200 km wide does not make it a planet, as asteroids range up to about 500 km and planets are nearly spherical. (v) Planet (one of the outer giants): it revolves around the Sun and is mostly gas and ice with flat ring-like structures, which is what the four large outer planets are like. Shining only by reflected sunlight does not make it a moon or a comet; all objects except the Sun shine that way. (Accept any other sound trap the student names for a card, with a correct reason.)
s: (i) natural satellite: moves around the Earth; cratered rock does not make it an asteroid
(ii) dwarf planet: IAU 2006 definition; once called a planet
(iii) comet: make-up and brightness near the Sun; shining does not make it a star
(iv) asteroid: small, rocky, irregular; 200 km is within the asteroid range
(v) planet (outer giant): reflected sunlight is true of every object except the Sun

questions.q:
Just after sunset, Kabir in Bhopal sees two bright objects in the western sky. One is a steady, very bright point; the other is fainter and has a long, faint tail stretching from it.
(a) Which one is most likely a comet and which is most likely Venus?
(b) Kabir's friend calls the steady point 'the Evening Star', so she says it is a star. Is she right? Give the clue from what Kabir saw.
questions.a: (a) The one with the tail is the comet; the steady, very bright point is likely Venus, which is seen shining brightly at dusk in the western sky. (b) No. Venus is a planet; it is called the Evening Star only because it shines brightly at dusk. The clue is that it shines steadily: stars appear to twinkle a lot, unlike planets.
s: Part (a): the tailed object is the comet, the steady bright point is Venus
Part (b): no, Venus is a planet; it shines steadily, while stars twinkle a lot

questions.q:
An observatory records a comet near the Sun in 1950 and again in 2003, and predicts its next return in 2056.
(a) Show that the gaps between its visits are equal.
(b) Compare this comet with Halley's Comet. Which of the two returns more often, and by how many years is its gap shorter?
(c) If it keeps the same pattern, in which year will this comet return after 2056?
questions.a: (a) 2003 - 1950 = 53 years and 2056 - 2003 = 53 years, so the gaps are equal. (b) Halley's Comet appears every 76 years, so this comet returns more often: 76 - 53 = 23 years shorter gap. (c) 2056 + 53 = 2109.
s: Part (a): both gaps are 53 years
Part (b): Halley's gap is 76 years; this comet, shorter by 76 - 53 = 23 years
Part (c): 2109

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Every comet that comes near the Sun returns to it again after a fixed time.
Reason (R): Many comets have been found that revolve around the Sun and approach close to it periodically.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is: 'It fell into Jupiter.' Write a question about a comet for which this is the correct answer. Then explain which of the kinds of comet journey described in the chapter it shows, and name the other two kinds.
questions.a: Example question: 'A comet approached Jupiter, the fifth planet from the Sun, and its path ran straight into the planet. Where did its journey end?' This shows that a few comets fall into the Sun or other planets when they approach them (some also break up). The other two journeys: many comets revolve around the Sun and come close to it periodically, and a few escape and move out of the Solar System.
s: A question about a comet whose answer is falling into Jupiter
Some comets break up or fall into the Sun or a planet
Others return periodically, and a few escape the Solar System

questions.q:
A space agency's list of four rocky objects that revolve around the Sun:
Object | Width | Where its path lies
A1 | 450 km | between the paths of Mars and Jupiter
A2 | 25 m | crosses the Earth's path
A3 | 3 m | crosses the Earth's path
A4 | 120 km | between the paths of Mars and Jupiter
All four are irregular in shape.
(a) Using the chapter's size range for asteroids, which of the four objects are of asteroid size? Show your check.
(b) What is the region where A1 and A4 revolve called?
(c) The agency can watch only one object closely: it must be an asteroid by the chapter's size range, and one that can come near our planet. A3 has a path just like A2's. Which object should it choose, and why not each of the others?
questions.a: (a) Asteroids are from 10 m to about 500 km across. A1 (450 km), A2 (25 m) and A4 (120 km) are in this range; A3 (3 m) is smaller than 10 m. (b) The asteroid belt (between Mars and Jupiter). (c) A2. Its path crosses the Earth's, so it can come near our planet, and at 25 m it is within the asteroid size range. A3 can come just as near but, at 3 m, is below the chapter's 10 m lower limit. A1 and A4 are asteroids, but they revolve in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, far from the Earth's path.
s: Part (a): A1, A2, A4 are within 10 m to 500 km; A3 is too small
Part (b): the asteroid belt
Part (c): A2, asteroid-sized with a path crossing the Earth's; A3 too small, A1 and A4 in the belt

questions.q: Tanvi was born in 2012. If Halley's Comet keeps to its usual return, about how old will she be at its next appearance?
questions.a: About 50 years old
o: About 50 years old
About 76 years old
About 26 years old
About 64 years old

questions.q:
A galaxy has millions to billions of stars.
(a) Is the Sun one of the stars of the Milky Way? Explain using the chapter.
(b) Are there stars that are not in the Milky Way at all? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Yes. The Sun is the star of our Solar System, and our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy, so the Sun is one of its many stars. (b) Yes. There are many galaxies in outer space beyond the Milky Way, and each galaxy has millions to billions of stars.
s: Part (a): yes, the Solar System (with the Sun) is part of the Milky Way
Part (b): yes, many other galaxies beyond, each with many stars

questions.q: In a class debate, Team A says, 'We are certainly alone in the Universe,' and Team B says, 'Scientists have already found life on other planets.' Evaluate both claims using the chapter, in five points, and give the conclusion the chapter supports.
questions.a: (1) Team A's claim is not supported: the chapter says we do not know yet whether life exists elsewhere in the Universe, so 'certainly alone' goes too far. (2) The Universe is very large: there are many galaxies beyond the Milky Way, and a galaxy has millions to billions of stars, so there is much still unexplored. (3) Team B's claim is also not supported: till now scientists have not found any evidence of life elsewhere. (4) The search for life has been directed mostly towards exoplanets, planets revolving around other stars in our galaxy, and this search is on and continuing. (5) Conclusion: both teams claim more than is known; the right answer today is 'we do not know yet'.
s: Team A goes too far: we do not know yet
The Universe has many galaxies with millions to billions of stars
Team B goes too far: no evidence of life found so far
The search is mostly towards exoplanets and is continuing
Conclusion: both overclaim; we do not know yet

questions.q: Imagine that the Sun suddenly stopped giving out light. Of the objects below, which one would still be seen shining in the night sky?
questions.a: Sirius, a star that shines by its own light
o: Sirius, a star that shines by its own light
Jupiter, a giant planet of gas and ice
Venus, the brightest object after the Moon
The Moon, our nearest neighbour in space

questions.q: A quiz asks: 'Which of these is not a member of our Solar System: Sirius, a comet, an asteroid, Pluto (which revolves around the Sun beyond Neptune)?' For each of the four, say whether it is a member and why.
questions.a: Sirius: not a member; it is a star outside our Solar System (the Sun is the only star of the Solar System). A comet: a member; comets are among the smaller objects that form the Solar System, and many revolve around the Sun. An asteroid: a member; asteroids revolve around the Sun, mostly in the asteroid belt. Pluto: a member; it revolves around the Sun beyond Neptune, though it is now called a dwarf planet, not a planet.
s: Sirius is not a member: a star outside the Solar System
Comet and asteroid are members, smaller objects revolving around the Sun
Pluto is a member, a dwarf planet revolving around the Sun

questions.q: Think of three places, from smaller to larger: our Solar System, the Milky Way Galaxy, the Universe. The Earth's Moon lies inside ___ of these three. (Write a number.)

True or False? 'From the same dark field in Spiti, a camper has a better chance of seeing the Milky Way on a moonless night than on a night when the bright Moon is up.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the Milky Way is seen as an extended faint band of light in the moonless night sky, viewed from dark locations away from city lights. A faint band is easily lost when the bright Moon lights up the sky.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the faint band is seen on moonless nights from dark places

questions.q:
A school science club in Kochi is making an exhibition stall called 'Is anyone out there?'. It has collected:
- Item 1: a report that astronomers have found a new planet X revolving around a star other than the Sun, in our galaxy.
- Item 2: a news website headline: 'Life confirmed on planet X!'
- Item 3: an observatory's statement: 'Planet X has been found. The search for signs of life goes on.'
- Item 4: a visitor's suggestion to feature the Moon instead, since India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near its south pole.
(a) What kind of object is planet X? Is it inside or outside our Solar System?
(b) Why is the Moon a poor place to look for life? Use the chapter.
(c) Which of Item 2 and Item 3 agrees with what the chapter says scientists know so far? Explain.
(d) The club must choose one main headline for the stall. Both are true: 'New planet found around another star!', which is exciting news, or 'Searching exoplanets for life: no evidence yet, the search goes on'. Decide which suits a stall called 'Is anyone out there?', weighing both.
questions.a: (a) An exoplanet: a planet discovered revolving around another star in our galaxy. It is outside our Solar System, since it does not revolve around the Sun (though it is inside the Milky Way). (b) There is hardly any atmosphere on the Moon, and the chapter says there is no atmosphere, water or life on it. (c) Item 3. The chapter says the search for life has been directed mostly towards exoplanets, and till now scientists have not found any evidence of life; the search is on and continuing. Item 2 claims more than is known. (d) The second headline. The first is true and exciting, but it says nothing about life, which is the stall's question, and visitors might wrongly take a new planet to mean life was found. The second answers the stall's question with what the chapter says scientists know: the search for life is directed mostly at exoplanets, no evidence has been found so far, and the search continues.
s: Part (a): an exoplanet, outside the Solar System (inside the Milky Way)
Part (b): hardly any atmosphere, no water or life on the Moon
Part (c): Item 3; no evidence of life found so far, search continuing
Part (d): the search headline, since it answers the stall's question about life; the planet headline is true but silent on life

questions.q: A science-fiction story says: 'Our spaceship flew out of the Milky Way Galaxy, and a few days later we landed on Jupiter.' What is wrong with the story?
questions.a: Jupiter is in the Solar System, inside the Milky Way
o: Jupiter is in the Solar System, inside the Milky Way
Nothing is wrong, since Jupiter lies in another galaxy
Jupiter lies in the asteroid belt, outside the Milky Way
Jupiter is a star, so no spaceship could ever land on it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Jupiter can be seen shining in the night sky with the naked eye.
Reason (R): Jupiter produces its own light, as the Sun does.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) Ritu writes in her project, 'Our Solar System is our galaxy.' Using the chapter, give the reason she is wrong.
(b) She then draws three nested boxes, each inside the one before: Universe, then Solar System, then Milky Way Galaxy. Correct the order of the boxes and justify each step from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Solar System is the Sun, eight planets, their moons, asteroids and comets: it has only one star, the Sun. A galaxy has millions to billions of stars, so the Solar System cannot be a galaxy. (b) The correct order is Universe, then Milky Way Galaxy, then Solar System. The Universe contains many galaxies beyond the Milky Way, so the Milky Way is one galaxy inside it; our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy, so it goes inside the Milky Way box.
s: Part (a): the Solar System has one star; a galaxy has millions to billions
Part (b): Universe, then Milky Way, then Solar System; many galaxies in the Universe, Solar System part of the Milky Way

questions.q: Zoya claims: 'Our whole Solar System is only a small part of something much bigger, and that bigger thing is itself only one of many.' Check her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy, which has millions to billions of stars, so the Solar System is only a small part of it. And the Milky Way is itself one of many galaxies: there are many galaxies in outer space beyond the Milky Way, all part of the Universe.
s: Verdict: yes, the claim is correct
The Solar System is a small part of the Milky Way, which has millions to billions of stars
The Milky Way is one of many galaxies in the Universe

questions.q:
Match each object in Column I with the description in Column II that places it correctly.
Column I | Column II
1. Halley's Comet | a. A member of our Solar System
2. Sirius | b. A star outside our Solar System that shines by its own light
3. An exoplanet | c. A planet revolving around a star other than the Sun, in our galaxy
4. A galaxy beyond ours | d. Part of the Universe, outside the Milky Way

Arjun has watched the night sky from his terrace in Chennai for years but has never seen the Milky Way. On a trip to a village in Ladakh he sees it clearly on a moonless night.
(a) Give two reasons from the chapter why he saw it in Ladakh but not in Chennai.
(b) Why does the Milky Way need these conditions more than a bright star like Sirius does?
questions.a: (a) The Milky Way is seen from dark locations away from city lights; the Ladakh village has almost no light pollution while the city has a lot, and the city sky is rarely clear because of smoke and dust. (b) The Milky Way appears only as a faint band of light, so it is easily washed out, while Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, so it can stand out where a faint band cannot.
s: Part (a): dark location away from city lights (no light pollution)
Part (a): clear sky without smoke and dust (or a moonless night)
Part (b): it is only a faint band, easily washed out; Sirius is the brightest star of the night sky

questions.q:

Line 1: Flat 12, Shivaji Nagar, Pune
Line 2: India
Line 3: Earth

(c) A scientist living (in a story) on an exoplanet writes the same kind of card. Which of Priya's Lines 4 to 6 would be different on the scientist's card, and which would be the same?
(d) A star in another galaxy is given the same kind of card. Which of Priya's six lines would it share with her? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Line 4: the Solar System; Line 5: the Milky Way Galaxy. (b) The Solar System is a part of the Milky Way Galaxy, so it is the smaller of the two and must come first. (c) An exoplanet revolves around a star other than the Sun, so Line 4 (our Solar System) would be different; it is in our galaxy, so Line 5 (the Milky Way) and Line 6 (the Universe) would be the same. (d) Only Line 6, the Universe. A star in another galaxy is outside the Milky Way, so it shares none of Lines 1 to 5; the many galaxies beyond the Milky Way are all part of the Universe, so Line 6 is shared.
s: Part (a): the Solar System, then the Milky Way Galaxy
Part (b): the Solar System is part of the Milky Way, so it comes first
Part (c): Line 4 differs; Lines 5 and 6 are the same
Part (d): only Line 6; another galaxy is outside the Milky Way but in the Universe

questions.q: Jupiter is called a giant planet. Compare the Sun and Jupiter on five points from the chapter: what kind of object each is and what it moves around; which is larger and heavier; where each gets its energy; what each is made of; and how each is seen from the Earth with the naked eye.
questions.a: (1) Kind and motion: the Sun is a star, the object that the planets revolve around; Jupiter is a planet that revolves around the Sun. (2) Size: Jupiter is much larger than the Earth, but the Sun is the largest and the heaviest object in the Solar System. (3) Energy: the Sun produces almost all the energy in the Solar System; Jupiter, like other planets, gets most of its energy from the Sun. (4) Made of: the Sun is an extremely hot ball of gases; Jupiter is mostly made of gas and ice, with flat ring-like structures of dust and rocky material. (5) Seen from the Earth: the Sun looks big and lights up the sky in the day; Jupiter can be seen with the naked eye only as a shining dot, since it is so far away.
s: Kind and motion: the Sun a star; Jupiter a planet revolving around the Sun
Size: Jupiter a giant, but the Sun is the largest and heaviest object
Energy: the Sun produces it; Jupiter gets most of its energy from the Sun
Made of: hot ball of gases vs mostly gas and ice with rings
Seen: the Sun lights the day; Jupiter only a shining dot, as it is far away
